Dr. Watson. The friend, companion, and narrator of the Sherlock Holmes stories. John Watson is a military physician who has returned wounded from the Second Afghan War. He rents rooms with Holmes at 221B Baker Street and chronicles the detective's cases through a series of tales that have made him as famous as his brilliant partner.

When Watson first arrives in London seeking lodgings, he meets Holmes and becomes the detective's closest confidant. His military experience and practical temperament ground him in reality, creating a sharp contrast with Holmes's pure intellect. Watson serves as the narrator of the Holmes cases, writing them as first-person accounts. This allows readers to experience the detective's genius alongside Watson's own amazement and skepticism at each new deduction.

Though Watson is less brilliant than Holmes, he is far from a mere dupe. His medical expertise proves useful in investigations, and his emotional life humanizes the narratives. His romantic inclinations, his frustrations, his occasional moral quandaries—these raise the stories above being pure logic puzzles. Watson is perceptive and capable, and he earns Holmes's genuine, if grudging, respect. His presence both tempers Holmes's eccentricity and deepens the detective's own humanity.

As chronicler, Watson raises interesting questions about narrative reliability and the nature of storytelling itself—questions that have become central to detective fiction's appeal. He helped define the companion-narrator trope that became foundational to the genre. Through Watson, we know the entire Holmes universe, and his affection for his friend and his narrative perspective frame the detective's cold logic.
